questions.stem: The gradient of a displacement-time graph gives the
questions.explanation: Gradient is change in the vertical quantity divided by change in the horizontal quantity, which here is $\frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}$ — displacement divided by time, which is velocity.

distractorRationale.a: Distance is read directly off the vertical axis, not from the gradient
distractorRationale.c: Acceleration is the gradient of a velocity-time graph, one derivative further on
distractorRationale.d: Momentum needs mass, which does not appear on either axis

questions.stem: A velocity-time graph is a horizontal straight line above the time axis. The body is

options.text: moving with uniform velocity and zero acceleration

questions.explanation: A horizontal line means the velocity value does not change with time, so the body keeps moving at a steady speed. The gradient of a horizontal line is zero, and gradient on this graph is acceleration, so the acceleration is zero.

distractorRationale.a: At rest would be a line lying along the time axis at v = 0, not above it
distractorRationale.b: Uniform acceleration would be a sloping straight line
distractorRationale.d: Deceleration would slope downwards towards the axis

questions.stem: The area between a velocity-time graph and the time axis represents the
questions.explanation: The area has units of velocity multiplied by time, that is $\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1} \times \text{s} = \text{m}$, so it must be a distance. Checking the units of an area or gradient is a reliable way to confirm what it represents.

distractorRationale.a: Acceleration is the gradient of this graph, not its area
distractorRationale.c: Average velocity is the area divided by the total time, so it is not the area itself
distractorRationale.d: Force requires mass, which is nowhere on this graph

questions.stem: On a velocity-time graph, a straight line rises from the origin to the point (10 s, 25 m/s). Calculate the acceleration of the body. Give your answer in metres per second squared.
questions.explanation: Acceleration is the gradient of the line: $a = \frac{25 - 0}{10 - 0} = 2.5\ \text{m/s}^2$. Because the line is straight, this acceleration is the same at every instant during the 10 s.

questions.stem: A bus accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 5.0 s, travels at 20 m/s for the next 10.0 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in a further 5.0 s. Calculate the total distance it travels. Give your answer in metres.
questions.explanation: The velocity-time graph is a trapezium of height 20 m/s, with the whole base 20 s long and the flat top 10 s long. Area $= \frac{1}{2}(20 + 10)(20) = \frac{1}{2}(30)(20) = 300\ \text{m}$. You can check it stage by stage: $50 + 200 + 50 = 300\ \text{m}$.

questions.stem: A section of a displacement-time graph is a horizontal straight line. During that section the body is
questions.explanation: A horizontal line means the displacement is not changing, so the body has not moved during that interval. Since gradient equals velocity and the gradient is zero, the velocity is zero and the body is at rest.

distractorRationale.a: That would be a sloping straight line — constant velocity means displacement changes steadily
distractorRationale.c: Uniform acceleration on this graph appears as a curve, not a straight line
distractorRationale.d: Moving backwards would give a line sloping downwards

questions.stem: A displacement-time graph is a curve whose steepness increases as time goes on. This tells us that the body is
questions.explanation: The gradient of a displacement-time graph is the velocity, so a curve that becomes steeper has an increasing gradient and therefore an increasing velocity. The body is accelerating.

distractorRationale.a: Slowing down would show as a curve that flattens out over time
distractorRationale.c: Uniform velocity gives a straight line of constant gradient
distractorRationale.d: Changing direction would show the curve turning back downwards

questions.stem: A velocity-time graph is a straight line passing through the points (0 s, 4 m/s) and (6 s, 28 m/s). Calculate the acceleration of the body. Give your answer in metres per second squared.
questions.explanation: Acceleration is the gradient: $a = \frac{28 - 4}{6 - 0} = \frac{24}{6} = 4\ \text{m/s}^2$. The line does not start at the origin, so you must subtract the initial velocity of 4 m/s rather than dividing 28 by 6.

questions.stem: A car decelerates uniformly from 30 m/s to 10 m/s over a period of 4.0 s. Using the area under the velocity-time graph, calculate the distance it covers during this time. Give your answer in metres.
questions.explanation: The graph section is a trapezium with parallel sides 30 m/s and 10 m/s and width 4.0 s. Area $= \frac{1}{2}(30 + 10)(4.0) = \frac{1}{2}(40)(4.0) = 80\ \text{m}$. This is the same as using the average velocity of 20 m/s for 4.0 s.

questions.stem: Part of a velocity-time graph lies below the time axis. This portion of the graph shows that the body is

options.text: moving in the direction opposite to its original motion

questions.explanation: Velocity is a vector, and the sign on the axis records its direction. A negative velocity therefore means the body is travelling the opposite way. The area below the axis is still a real distance, but it is a displacement in the negative direction, so it is subtracted when finding total displacement.

distractorRationale.a: At rest corresponds to the line lying exactly on the axis, where v = 0
distractorRationale.c: Unlimited acceleration would show as an ever-steepening curve, not a position below the axis
distractorRationale.d: The graph axes are velocity and time; they carry no information about height or position in space

questions.stem: What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph represent?
questions.explanation: The gradient of a velocity-time graph indicates how velocity changes with respect to time, which is defined as acceleration. A steeper gradient means a greater rate of change of velocity.

distractorRationale.a: Displacement is represented by the area under the velocity-time graph, not the gradient.
distractorRationale.b: Velocity is represented by the value on the vertical axis of the graph, not the gradient.
distractorRationale.d: Distance is calculated from the area under the velocity-time graph, not the gradient.

questions.stem: A velocity-time graph shows a triangular area under the curve between 0 s and 4 s, where the velocity varies linearly from 0 m/s to 16 m/s. What is the distance traveled during this time?

questions.stem: A car moves with a velocity of 10 m/s for 5 seconds and then accelerates uniformly to a velocity of 30 m/s over the next 5 seconds. What is the total distance covered by the car during the entire motion?
questions.explanation: The distance covered at constant velocity is 10 m/s * 5 s = 50 m. For the acceleration phase, the average velocity is (10 m/s + 30 m/s) / 2 = 20 m/s, so the distance covered is 20 m/s * 5 s = 100 m. Total distance = 50 m + 100 m = 150 m.

distractorRationale.a: 50 m is only the distance covered at constant velocity.
distractorRationale.c: 100 m is only the distance covered during the acceleration phase.
distractorRationale.d: 125 m does not accurately reflect the total distance traveled.

questions.stem: A cyclist travels at a speed of 12 m/s for 4 seconds and then slows down to a stop in 2 seconds. Calculate the total distance covered by the cyclist.

distractorRationale.a: 48 m is only the distance covered while traveling at constant speed.
distractorRationale.b: 24 m does not reflect the correct calculations for both phases of motion.
distractorRationale.d: 60 m is the total distance, but the options must be carefully calculated to find the correct answer.
